prompt.context: Balke-Collender Corp. (NYSE: BCC) is a publicly traded chemical company. Several Chinese companies have entered the market since 2008, putting enormous pressure on BCC's bottom line. As a result, BCC stock has stagnated around $48 since 2010. Raider Capital Partners (RCP), an infamous Wall Street activist investor, has taken a 14% stake in BCC and is threatening to change the board and fire the CEO, unless he brings up the stock price. The CEO has asked us two questions: (1) How can we achieve 100% total shareholder return (TSR) within 5 years to get RCP off our back? (2) How can we restore the company's long-term competitiveness?
prompt.question: How can BCC achieve 100% total shareholder return (TSR) within 5 years, and how can it restore long-term competitiveness?

clarifying_info.q: What is BCC's current P/E ratio?
clarifying_info.a: BCC has a P/E ratio of 20.

clarifying_info.q: How many shares does BCC have outstanding?
clarifying_info.a: BCC has 125 million fully-diluted shares outstanding.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market demand for ethylene?
clarifying_info.a: Current demand for ethylene is 210 million tons.

clarifying_info.q: Are there opportunities to cut SG&A?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no opportunities to cut SG&A.
All D&A comes from the ethylene cracker.
Yes, the company has the ability to raise debt.

clarifying_info.q: What is ethylene and how is it made?
clarifying_info.a: Ethylene is a petrochemical used in a wide variety of applications. It is made from a variety of hydrocarbons; the most common feedstocks are naphtha (derived from oil production), ethane and propane (both derived from natural gas).

exhibits.title: BCC Income Statement
exhibits.shows: BCC's income statement in $ millions, showing revenue, COGS, gross income, SG&A, D&A, operating income, interest, EBT, tax, and net income line items. A note states BCC depreciates assets over a 10-year period using the straight-line method.

exhibits.title: Ethylene Cost Curve
exhibits.shows: A market cost curve plotting variable cost ($/ton) on the y-axis against cumulative capacity (million tons) on the x-axis for all industry participants: Alpha Chem, Beta Chem, Gamma Chem, BCC, Delta Chem, Epsilon Chem, Omega Chem. Companies are labeled as using either ethane feedstock crackers or naphtha feedstock crackers.

exhibits.title: Estimated VC Breakdown at BCC Plant
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing variable cost per ton breakdown for naphtha vs. ethane feedstock at BCC, broken down into components: Feedstock, Freight-In, Power, and Freight-Out.

data.key_difference: Feedstock cost is much higher for naphtha than ethane

exhibits.title: Investment Options
exhibits.shows: A table listing three investment options — Feedstock Conversion, Capacity Expansion, and Both — with their respective plant investment, pipeline investment, incremental fixed cost, and change in capacity figures.

framework: Increase Share Price: drive EPS growth or P/E multiple expansion
Increase EPS: grow net income or reduce fully-diluted shares outstanding (FDSO)
Grow Net Income via Revenue: increase capacity or improve pricing
Grow Net Income via Cost Reduction: decrease variable costs (feedstock) or decrease fixed costs
Decrease FDSO: share buybacks funded by leverage or asset sales
Increase P/E Multiple: reduce cost of capital, increase leverage, improve growth narrative
Return Capital to Investors: increase dividends, sell non-core divisions

questions.prompt: What is the incremental net income required to achieve 100% TSR (doubling the share price)?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work backward from share price using P/E ratio to find current net income, then set the required net income at 2x current to double the share price (holding P/E constant). Key formula: EPS = Share Price / P/E; Net Income = EPS x FDSO.

math.setup: Share Price = $48; P/E = 20; FDSO = 125M shares. Target: 100% TSR means share price doubles to $96, so EPS must double from $2.40 to $4.80, requiring Net Income to double from $300M to $600M.
steps: Net Income = EPS x FDSO = 2.40 x 125M = $300M

questions.prompt: What is the market price of ethylene, and what does BCC's cost structure look like?
questions.guidance: Because total industry demand is 210M tons and BCC is the marginal (highest-cost) producer needed to meet demand, prices are set so the next entrant (Delta Chem at ~$650/ton VC) makes zero profit. Price is therefore just under $750/ton (candidate may use $750). BCC capacity is 20M tons (Revenue $15B / $750 = 20M units). Total VC = $550 x 20M = $11B; COGS is $13B, implying $2B in fixed COGS (labor, overhead). Candidates must recognize that taxes, interest, and D&A cannot be changed, leaving four levers: expand capacity, decrease variable costs (feedstock switch), decrease fixed costs (tied to plant layout), or cut SG&A (no scope).

math.setup: Revenue = $15,000M; assume price = $750/ton; COGS = $13,000M; VC per ton (naphtha) = $550.
math.answer: BCC produces 20M tons at $750/ton; fixed COGS = $2B; four improvement levers identified

questions.prompt: What is the value of each of the three investment options (Feedstock Conversion, Capacity Expansion, Both)?
questions.guidance: Candidate must build an incremental income statement for each option. Key insight: expanding capacity by 20M tons makes Delta Chem the new marginal producer, dropping price from $750 to $650/ton. Feedstock conversion to ethane reduces VC from $550 to $350/ton. Compare net income increments for each option. Feedstock Conversion and Both achieve the same net income (+$900M), but Feedstock Conversion requires lower total investment ($25B vs $35B), giving it higher NPV. Recommend Feedstock Conversion.

math.setup: Current: 20M tons at $750/ton, VC=$550, Fixed COGS=$2B, D&A=$500M, Tax rate=40% implied. Incremental analysis for each option using data from Exhibit 4.
steps: Feedstock Conversion only (no new capacity, price stays $750): Contribution = (750-350) x 20M = $8,000M; FC = -$4,000M; Gross Income = $4,000M; D&A = -$2,500M; Tax = -$600M; Net Income = $900M; Total Investment = $10B+$15B = $25B

Capacity Expansion only (add 20M tons, price drops to $650, VC stays $550): Contribution = (650-550) x 20M = $4,000M; FC = -$2,000M; Gross Income = $2,000M; D&A = -$1,500M; Tax = -$200M; Net Income = $300M; Total Investment = $15B

Both (add 20M tons at $650, VC drops to $350): Contribution = (650-350) x 20M = $12,000M; FC = -$7,000M; Gross Income = $5,000M; D&A = -$3,500M; Tax = -$600M; Net Income = $900M; Total Investment = $20B+$15B = $35B
Feedstock Conversion vs Both: same net income ($900M), but Feedstock Conversion requires $25B vs $35B investment → higher NPV for Feedstock Conversion
math.answer: Feedstock Conversion: Net Income +$900M (investment $25B). Capacity Expansion: Net Income +$300M (investment $15B). Both: Net Income +$900M (investment $35B). Choose Feedstock Conversion.

brainstorming.prompt: What is the price of ethylene in the market?

categories.name: Marginal Producer Pricing Logic
ideas: Total industry demand is 210M tons; BCC is the marginal (last needed) producer
Prices are set so the next producer (Delta Chem at ~$650/ton VC) earns zero profit and has no incentive to enter
Market price is therefore just under $750/ton (candidate may use $750/ton)
BCC at 20M tons capacity and $750/ton revenue implies full utilization

categories.name: Cost Structure Implications
ideas: BCC's current VC of $550/ton (naphtha) is higher than ethane-based competitors
Fixed COGS of $2B per year (labor, overhead) separate from variable costs
D&A of $500M tied to existing cracker asset base

categories.name: Levers to Improve Performance
ideas: Expand capacity (shifts marginal producer, changes price — see Exhibit 3)
Decrease VC by switching feedstock from naphtha to ethane (see Exhibit 3)
Decrease fixed COGS (tied to plant layout, overlaps with capacity option)
Reduce taxes or interest (structural, limited lever)

recommendation: Convert BCC's current plant to ethane feedstock at a total investment of $25B ($10B plant + $15B pipeline)
This generates $900M improvement in net income, increasing EPS by approximately 3x current level and exceeding the 100% TSR target
Feedstock conversion is preferred over the 'Both' option because it achieves the same net income improvement ($900M) at lower investment ($25B vs $35B), delivering higher NPV
risks: Competitors (especially Delta Chem) may also switch to ethane feedstock, eroding relative cost advantage
Ethane/natural gas prices may rise, reducing the feedstock cost differential
Significant capital requirement ($25B) increases leverage and financial risk
Plant downtime during conversion will temporarily reduce revenue and earnings
Supply chain disruption risk during pipeline construction
next_steps: Determine competitor reaction: can and will Delta Chem or others also switch to ethane, and how will this affect relative cost positions?
Secure appropriate financing to retool the ethylene cracker ($25B total)
Quantify the effects of downtime for all three options and refine NPV calculations
Assess pipeline routing feasibility and permitting timeline
Model sensitivity of returns to ethane price movements
